background.definition: Cat scratch disease (CSD), also called bartonellosis, is an infection with Bartonella henselae that produces a subacute, solitary, or regional lymphadenopathy in a patient exposed to a cat or kitten scratch, bite, or saliva. Typical CSD encompasses regional or isolated lymphadenopathy. Atypical CSD encompasses systemic spread of B. henselae with organ involvement.

list.listitem: The estimated annual incidence is 4.0/100,000 people in the United States.
CSD usually presents in children and adolescents younger than 18 years, but can occur at any age.
Although B. henselae is prevalent worldwide, there is a higher prevalence in warmer climates where the cat flea can survive year round.
The incidence of CSD is higher during autumn and winter because of the seasonal breeding of the domestic cat.
CSD is the third most common cause of fever of unknown origin in children.
One case report outlined reactivation of an atypical B. henselae infection associated with COVID-19 infection.
The Bartonella species most commonly responsible for CSD is B. henselae and, to a lesser degree, Bartonella quintana.
Domestic cats are the natural reservoir for the Bartonella species.
Transmission from cats to humans usually occurs by a scratch or a bite and is caused by the presence of the bacterium on the cat’s claws or in the oral cavity.
Direct human-to-human transmission has not been reported.
CSD is caused by the intracellular, fastidious, Gram-negative bacillus B. henselae and, to a lesser extent, B. quintana.
Following inoculation, there is an incubation period, which is followed by a period of self-limited febrile illness with lymphadenopathy.
Diagnosis should be suspected in patients with regional lymphadenopathy 1 to 3 weeks after exposure to a cat, especially if it follows an erythematous vesiculopapular eruption. C
Use indirect fluorescent antibody testing for B. henselae to confirm the diagnosis in all suspected cases. An IgG of greater than 1:256 is considered indicative of current or recent infection. C
PCR of lymph node aspirates, if available, are also an option, although the sensitivity of PCR varies widely.C

Imaging tests are not generally useful in confirming the diagnosis. They should be used to evaluate atypical or complicated cases involving visceral organs (eg, liver ultrasound to evaluate hepatic granulomata, and cardiac echocardiography to evaluate endocarditis). C

list.listitem: A careful history of close contact with a cat or kitten 1 to 3 weeks ago is crucial.

The primary lesion (a painless, erythematous vesicle in the scratch line) appears 3 to 10 days after the inciting cat bite or scratch. Over the next 5 to 7 days, the lesion transforms to a reddish-brown, discrete papule that persists for 2 to 3 weeks. Patients frequently ignore these lesions; therefore, it is important to ask patients if they noticed any unusual skin lesions.
Solitary or regional lymphadenopathy develops over 2 to 3 weeks and typically persists for 1 to 3 months.
Affected lymph nodes are commonly fluctuant and tender to palpation. The duration of lymphadenopathy is typically 1 to 3 months, but may persist up to a year.
Patients may have low-grade fevers and night sweats.

Atypical manifestations include malaise, arthralgias, skin eruptions, weight loss, Parinaud’s oculoglandular syndrome (unilateral conjunctivitis with adjacent periauricular lymphadenopathy), splenic or hepatic granulomas, encephalopathy, neuroretinitis, endocarditis, and pleural and pericardial effusions.
Commonly used laboratory tests are not useful. Serologic tests only help confirm clinical suspicion.
The indirect fluorescent antibody test is used to confirm the diagnosis in suspected cases.

The overall sensitivity of the indirect fluorescent antibody test is 88% and the specificity is 97% (LR+ 29, LR− 0.12); however, these numbers are nonuniform and dependent upon the antigen used or the cutoff chosen.
An indirect fluorescent antibody IgG >1:256 is considered indicative of current or recent infection.
A positive indirect fluorescent antibody IgM generally indicates recent or current infection, but false-positive results are associated with recent Epstein-Barr viral infections.
PCR of lymph node aspirates are also an option, although generally only done if lymph node aspiration is being done to relieve pain.

Tissue or blood cultures are impractical since the organism is very slow growing, requiring a 6-week incubation time. Live organisms are rarely isolated from the blood or tissues of infected patients.

Imaging tests are not useful in confirming the diagnosis. Targeted imaging studies should be used to evaluate atypical or complicated cases; for example, liver ultrasound to evaluate hepatic granulomata, and cardiac echocardiography to evaluate endocarditis.
The diagnosis of CSD is based largely upon clinical suspicion.
Indirect fluorescent antibody serology confirms a clinical suspicion of CSD.
Treatment is symptomatic in uncomplicated cases.
The treatment is symptomatic (with analgesics) in immunocompetent persons. C
A 5-day course of azithromycin will decrease the volume of lymphadenopathy and decrease pain in half of those who take it, but there are no benefits in terms of outcomes or time to resolution. B
Fine-needle aspiration of a painful lymph node may help relieve pressure and pain. C
Incision and drainage may be useful in severe cases involving suppurative lymph nodes and pain not relieved by fine-needle aspiration. C
Systemic and atypical CSD may respond to antibiotics (eg, macrolide, tetracyclines). C
Typical CSD is usually self-limited and does not require antibiotic therapy in immunocompetent persons; it typically resolves in 2 to 4 months without specific treatment.
Symptomatic treatment with analgesics is recommended.

A 5-day course of azithromycin will decrease the volume of lymphadenopathy and decrease pain in half of those who take it, but it has not been shown to reduce time to resolution. Azithromycin has also been anecdotally recommended for severe CSD or systemic disease. The dose is 500 mg on day 1 and 250 mg on days 2 to 5 for adults and children weighing more than 45 kg (100 lbs) and 10 mg/kg on day 1 followed by 5 mg/kg on days 2 to 5 for those weighing less.
Corticosteroids have been used anecdotally in some patients with no demonstrable efficacy in typical or atypical/systemic manifestations of Bartonella infections.
Gentamicin, ciprofloxacin, rifampin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole have all been anecdotally recommended in patients with liver or spleen involvement.
Doxycycline and rifampin have been anecdotally recommended in patients with neuroretinitis.
Experts recommend beta-lactam antibiotics (amoxacillin or ceftriaxone) with gentamicin or combined with doxycycline for infective endocarditis.
Fine-needle aspiration of a painful lymph node may help relieve pressure and pain.

Incision and drainage may be useful in severe cases involving suppurative lymph nodes and pain not relieved by fine-needle aspiration. The risk of incision and drainage is chronic drainage and fistula formation.
Immunocompromised patients with systemic forms of CSD should be referred to an infectious disease specialist.
Immunocompromised patients with systemic disease should be hospitalized.
Most cases of typical CSD are self-limited without long-term sequellae. B
CSD affects the elderly (>60 years). Atypical clinical presentations are more common in, but are not limited to, the elderly and immunocompromised patients.
Lymphadenopathy is less common in elderly patients; fatigue and malaise are more common.
Atypical CSD in the elderly include fever of unknown origin, encephalitis, and endocarditis.
Diagnosis is delayed for more than 6 weeks in the elderly twice as often as it is in younger patients: a clinical index of suspicion is crucial to diagnosis.
